analysis.one_liner: Puts payments on Treasury bonds ahead of every other federal obligation if the debt limit is hit.
analysis.headline: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar one day after its January 2011 introduction but never received a vote, dying when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: If the federal debt hit its legal ceiling, this bill would have required the Treasury Department to pay the principal and interest on debt held by the public before any other obligation the government owes. Everyone else the government owes — Social Security recipients, troops and federal workers, hospitals billing Medicare, contractors — would legally come second. The bill never got a Senate vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from January 26, 2011 until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of U.S. Treasury securities — big banks, money market funds, foreign governments, and investors — would be guaranteed payment with legal priority over every other obligation, even in a debt-ceiling standoff.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Treasury bondholders — banks, funds, foreign governments

how_it_helps.text: If the debt reached its statutory limit, the Treasury's authority to pay principal and interest on debt held by the public would 'take priority over all other obligations' the government has incurred.

That would assure creditors who hold Treasury securities that they get paid even if other government obligations — benefit checks, payroll, contractor invoices — go unpaid during a debt-limit impasse.

analysis.who_pays: Social Security recipients, veterans, active-duty troops, federal employees, Medicare providers, and government contractors, who would legally wait behind bondholders for their money during any debt-ceiling standoff.

drawbacks.text: The bill would subordinate every government obligation except Treasury bond payments — including Social Security, Medicare, military pay, and money owed to federal contractors — during a debt-limit crisis.

Prioritizing bond payments does not resolve a debt-ceiling standoff; it would remove the pressure on Congress to fix the impasse by guaranteeing that creditors are made whole first, leaving everyone else unpaid longer.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill protects only one class of obligations: it shields Treasury creditors from any risk while doing nothing for the beneficiaries and workers the government also owes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would protect one narrow class — Treasury creditors — from the consequences of a debt-ceiling standoff while pushing the entire cost onto everyone else the government owes. It would not solve the underlying impasse; it would simply decide who is harmed first. For ordinary people the trade is poor: certain, legally protected payment for bondholders, and uncertainty for their own benefits and pay.

outcome.mechanism: It was placed on the Senate calendar a day after introduction but was never brought up for a vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Toomey introduced the Full Faith and Credit Act in the Senate on January 25, 2011.
The bill was read the second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 2 on January 26, 2011.
Twenty-two senators cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee vote, no floor debate, no roll-call — and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, no law was ever enacted putting bondholders ahead of Social Security recipients, troops, federal workers, and contractors. Everyone the government owes other than Treasury holders avoided being legally demoted to second in line; bondholders did not get their priority locked in.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone the government owes except bondholders

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 25, 2011.

for.name: 22 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 22 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar for the full two years of the 112th Congress.

against.name: Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner
against.what_they_did: Publicly argued during the 2011 debt-limit standoff that the government could not practically pick and choose which obligations to pay, undercutting the bill's premise.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill never attracted a Democratic sponsor; no vote was ever held, so there was no recorded roll-call to confirm a party split.

industries.industry: Holders of U.S. Treasury securities (banks, money market funds, foreign governments, investors)
industries.note: The bill would give these creditors first claim on federal money, guaranteed by statute, even in a fiscal standoff. Their assured payment would come directly at the expense of Social Security recipients, troops, federal workers, and contractors who would be paid after them.

In a debt-limit crisis, payments owed to contractors would rank behind Treasury bond payments, so vendors could wait indefinitely while bondholders are paid. They would share the public's fate rather than profit from the bill.
